articles.title: Leilão em Ipatinga tem motos 2025 e carros a partir de R$ 600 | G1
articles.standfirst: São 252 lotes, incluindo 98 veículos recuperáveis, entre carros e motos. Interessados podem visitar o Pátio Vale do Aço até sexta-feira (16). O leilão on-line será de 20 a 22 de outubro.
articles.summary: Leilão do Detran-MG reúne 252 lotes em Ipatinga, com carros, motos e sucatas. Visitação começa nesta quarta (14). Veja valores e como participar.
articles.body:
Moto 2025 e carro com lance inicial de R$ 600 fazem parte dos lotes no leilão em Ipatinga — Foto: Divulgação/Detran-MG

Motos fabricadas em 2025, um Renault Kwid 2021 e carros com lances iniciais de R$ 600 estão entre os veículos disponíveis no leilão do Departamento Estadual de Trânsito de Minas Gerais (Detran-MG), em Ipatinga , no Leste de Minas. A visitação presencial começou e segue até sexta-feira (16). Ao todo, são 252 lotes disponíveis para arrematação.

Segundo o edital , são 98 veículos classificados como recuperáveis , sendo 41 carros e 57 motocicletas. Os outros 154 lotes são sucatas , destinadas ao aproveitamento de peças e que não podem voltar a circular.

Entre os modelos mais recentes estão três motocicletas Honda CG 160 fabricadas em 2025, com lances iniciais de R$ 3 mil a R$ 4 mil. A lista também inclui um Renault Kwid 2021, com avaliação inicial de R$ 10 mil, e um Hyundai i30 2010, pelo mesmo valor.

Entre os automóveis com menores avaliações estão um Ford Focus Ghia 2001, com lance inicial de R$ 600, um Fiat Uno S 1990, por R$ 700, e um GM Celta 2005, também por R$ 700.

Os valores são os preços mínimos de avaliação dos veículos. O preço final será definido pelos lances apresentados durante o leilão.

Veículos conservados: veja alguns modelos e valores

Os veículos classificados como recuperáveis são aqueles que podem voltar a circular após o cumprimento das exigências de regularização previstas no Código de Trânsito Brasileiro.

Entre os automóveis com maiores avaliações iniciais estão:

Entre as motocicletas mais recentes estão:

A lista também inclui motocicletas recuperáveis com avaliações menores, como uma Suzuki EN125 Yes 2008, com lance inicial de R$ 600.

Além dos 98 veículos recuperáveis, o leilão reúne 154 lotes classificados como sucata. Diferentemente dos conservados, esses veículos não podem voltar a circular e são destinados ao aproveitamento de peças.

Segundo o edital do Detran-MG, há duas categorias: sucatas aproveitáveis, cujas peças podem ser reutilizadas em outros veículos, e sucatas aproveitáveis com motor inservível, que possuem restrições adicionais para o reaproveitamento do motor.

Entre os lotes classificados como sucata, estão:

Shineray XY 50 Q, 2011: lance inicial de R$ 100.

Ford Escort L, 1988: lance inicial de R$ 150.

GM Celta 4P Life, 2006: lance inicial de R$ 150.

Fiat Uno S, 1990: lance inicial de R$ 200.

Fiat Palio EDX, 1996: lance inicial de R$ 300.

Honda CBX 250 Twister, 2002: lance inicial de R$ 300.

A participação na disputa por sucatas é restrita a compradores que atendam às exigências de credenciamento previstas no edital. Os valores apresentados são avaliações iniciais, e não preços finais de arrematação.

Os interessados poderão conferir pessoalmente os veículos entre os dias 14 e 16 de outubro, das 9h às 12h e das 13h às 16h, no Pátio Vale do Aço, localizado na Avenida José Anatólio Barbosa, nº 2017, bairro Limoeiro, em Ipatinga.

A visitação permite apenas a inspeção visual dos veículos. Não será permitido manusear os bens ou realizar reparos no local. O edital também proíbe a entrada com mochilas, bolsas e capacetes .

As datas foram confirmadas pelo Detran-MG após a publicação de uma errata no Diário Oficial Minas Gerais, em 29 de setembro de 2026. O documento corrigiu o período de visitação e as datas do leilão.

O leilão será realizado exclusivamente pela internet, por meio do Sistema de Leilão de Veículos do Detran-MG, entre os dias 20 e 22 de outubro.

A sessão terá início às 8h do dia 20 e será encerrada às 18h do dia 22.

Para participar, os interessados devem realizar um cadastro no sistema eletrônico do Detran-MG .

É necessário apresentar documento de identificação, CPF ou CNPJ, comprovante de endereço, e-mail e telefone, conforme as exigências do edital. Pessoas jurídicas também devem apresentar a documentação de constituição da empresa.

O cadastro passa por análise da comissão responsável, que tem até cinco dias úteis para liberar o acesso. A confirmação é enviada por e-mail.

Após a aprovação, os participantes poderão apresentar lances eletrônicos nos lotes disponíveis. Vence quem oferecer o maior valor aceito para cada veículo.

A participação é permitida a pessoas físicas e jurídicas, respeitadas as regras do edital . Para adquirir sucatas, é necessário credenciamento específico junto ao Detran-MG.

O pagamento dos veículos arrematados deverá ser feito à vista, por meio do Documento de Arrecadação Estadual (DAE), em até três dias úteis após o encerramento do leilão.

A relação completa dos veículos, os valores iniciais e as regras de participação estão disponíveis no edital nº 1668/2026 e no Sistema de Leilão de Veículos do Detran-MG.

articles.title: Bank of America CEO reveals how US’ second-largest bank had to hire thousands and spend millions of dollars to ‘contain’ damage done by Anthropic’s AI Agent Mythos
articles.summary: America's second-largest bank, Bank of America (BoFA), may have just told everyone how dangerous AI agents can be for companies.
articles.body: America's second-largest bank, Bank of America (BoFA), may have just told everyone how dangerous AI agents can be for companies. According to Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan, the bank has enlisted an army of external contractors and deployed thousands of tech workers to fortify its code against emerging cybersecurity threats posed by frontier artificial intelligence. CEO Brian Moynihan revealed the same in an interview with CNBC.The defensive overhaul was reportedly triggered after advanced AI Agents, including Anthropic’s Mythos -- demonstrated a heightened capacity to pinpoint and exploit longstanding software vulnerabilities across bank's internal and vendor networks. “That risk is real risk, and that’s why when the frontier-type models came out... a lot of us sat down and said, ‘How do we figure out how to get through this quickly?’” Moynihan told CNBC’s Leslie Picker following the release of the bank’s third-quarter earnings.To deal with an immediate threat, the bank hired 1,000 third-party contractors during the second quarter. Those specialists joined 3,000 existing internal staff dedicated to software maintenance and security, Moynihan said, and they remain actively engaged in remediation efforts.The emergency response meant a substantial cost for the bank. Moynihan told analysts that the bank incurred a "couple hundred million plus" in expenses during the third quarter alone, tied to the software patching campaign alongside anti-money laundering regulatory compliance measures.Moynihan’s remarks offer an unusually transparent glimpse into the tangible dollar and labor costs that major US financial institutions face as they confront the unintended fallout of rapid AI innovation. Mythos was distributed in April to a select cohort of banks, technology firms, and government agencies, setting off an urgent defensive scramble across corporate America to remediate decades-old coding gaps before malicious actors could take advantage of similar frontier tooling.“We’ve got to stay ahead of them, and we’ve got to be mindful that the people doing the software development are the people trying to sell us the services,” Moynihan said.The spending disclosures comes against a challenging market backdrop, with Bank of America shares sliding as much as 8%. Addressing investor concerns over escalating overhead, Moynihan emphasized that the surge in cybersecurity contracting would be temporary. “Once you patch, you don’t have to patch as much... the pipeline moves through,” Moynihan said, noting that remediation expenses are projected to taper off once core vulnerabilities are sealed.'Bank of America is replacing only 75% of employees who leave'Even as the bank absorbs short-term defensive costs, it is actively leaning on AI to drive broader operating efficiencies. Bank of America currently operates roughly 130 internal AI initiatives. The bank expects annual cost savings generated by those systems to jump from $300 million this year to $700 million by 2027.Over the past year, the lender reduced its overall workforce by roughly 3,400 positions, a drawdown that included shedding about 5% of its management ranks. Speaking at an event, Brian said that BofA has an employee attrition rate ranging from 8% to 8.5%. Based on current headcount, the implication is that around 1,400 people leave each month, at least. When they do, he said that the Bank only replaces 1,000 of them. The other 300 jobs must be 'owned' he said. More prosaically, they must be done by existing staff.Fortunately, AI is around to help with this. "In the end of day, our teammates have got to use AI to make our company better and make our clients a better experience," declared Moynihan. BofA now has "150 use cases implemented" and is deploying AI into "more work," he said too. This work includes audit, legal and other areas. And BofA's 18,000 coders have "saved" 10-15%, which is being redeployed.Bank of America fined $1.2 billionThe US government has imposed a $1.2 billion fine on America’s second-biggest bank. The amount is the third-largest in the department’s history. “When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement. “Today’s actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law.”In a statement, Treasury said that its Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed the $1.2 billion penalty for Bank of America’s “failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border."“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,’’ Bank of America said in a statement. It added, “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators."You use AI every day. articles.title: Israeli ad company helped a spyware firm target Al Jazeera through online ads, researchers say
articles.summary: An Israeli ad company, DiscoverTech, has for years been secretly helping spyware developers place their hacking software on popular websites, researchers say.
articles.body: An Israeli ad company, DiscoverTech, has for years been secretly helping spyware developers place their hacking software on popular websites, researchers at Citizen Lab say, resulting in a cyberattack that targeted at least 45 devices at the news outlet Al Jazeera. The findings, documented in a report published Thursday by Citizen Lab, are the first time cybersecurity experts have shown how online ad platforms, so common across the internet that they are inescapable, can be used as a vector to hack visitors’ devices without their knowledge. “Any time we browse the internet or open an app, all the data on our device can be hacked by malicious actors without us even knowing,” said Natalia Krapiva, a spyware expert at the digital rights nonprofit Access Now, who read the report and was not involved with its research. “States and tech companies whose infrastructure is used to conduct these attacks need to take urgent technical, legal and regulatory measures.” The report is a joint effort between Confiant, a U.S. ad security company, and the Citizen Lab, a University of Toronto operation that researches mercenary spyware computer programs. Spyware is often leased to governments around the world to help them hack devices of people they want to spy on. While spyware companies often tout their products as crucial tools for governments to enforce national security, the tech has repeatedly been used around the world to crack down on journalists, human rights advocates and political opposition. DiscoverTech is a Tel Aviv company that sells online advertising services, the report said. “We take pride in providing our clients with a gateway to global fraud-free traffic, connecting your brand with real users,” its site says. DiscoverTech is one of a number of companies that help brands show their advertisements on websites that may be visited by potential customers. But the company secretly ran a separate program, the report says, that allowed spyware companies to inject malicious software onto visitors’ devices. The malicious code used to hack Al Jazeera computers was particularly effective, the researchers said, because it was “no-click” spyware — meaning a victim did not need to download a file or even click a link to be infected, just visit a website with a vulnerable computer and see the ad. The hacks, which were not previously reported until the release of the Citizen Lab’s report, occurred in 2024 and 2025. Al Jazeera provided the Citizen Lab with network logs from the period of the attacks, which researchers used to reconstruct how they unfolded, the Citizen Lab said in the report. It previously reported that the phones of 36 Al Jazeera journalists and staff members had been hacked with what it said was Pegasus spyware made by a different Israeli company, NSO Group, most likely by operators linked to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. NSO said at the time that it would review the findings. Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment. Neither did DiscoverTech and its CEO. Like many advertising platforms, DiscoverTech has a wide reach: The report said it serves ads on almost 200,000 websites, Android apps and iOS apps, including those of major media organizations, search engines, government agencies and dating services. The report says Confiant detected DiscoverTech ads served on networks of major government entities like those of the U.S. Defense Department and the Dutch Economic Affairs Ministry, though it emphasized that the presence of ads does not indicate those organizations were targeted in malicious campaigns. Five ad vendors and industry organizations responded to the Citizen Lab’s findings by disconnecting DiscoverTech from their platforms. A Google spokesperson told NBC News that Google had helped the Citizen Lab and Confiant in their investigation and affirmed their findings, saying DiscoverTech is now banned on Google Ads. A spokesperson for IAB Europe, the continent’s largest trade organization for the advertising industry, said it has suspended DiscoverTech from its platforms. The report said the ad platforms Beeswax, Vungle and Eskimi took similar action. The online advertising industry is a vast, convoluted and largely unregulated system that relies on maintaining significant technical information about people. Websites rarely directly control which companies post ads on their sites. Instead, advertisers preprogram “bids” for every person who visits and often prefer to advertise to people matching certain characteristics so their ads can be more targeted. The industry usually refrains from collecting specific personal information on people, but it assigns them industry “advertising IDs” and ties information like age, sex, location and preferences to them. The researchers say DiscoverTech taps into that system to offer a secret program called Controlium, which allows spyware companies to use DiscoverTech’s ad network to identify people to hack and help them deliver the malicious code to take over their devices. Controlium is not mentioned on DiscoverTech’s website, but researchers say they found source code on its login pages and were able to view aspects of how the program works. It allowed users to pick specific people to infect or profile using their phones’ advertising IDs, browser identifiers or IP addresses, numbers assigned to internet connections that can help tie people to locations such as their homes. The researchers found that Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that now operates as Integrity Labs, used DiscoverTech’s ads to deliver its spyware. The U.S. Commerce Department added Candiru to its Entity List in 2021, saying foreign governments had used its software to target journalists, activists and government officials. Wolfie Christl, one of the Citizen Lab researchers behind the report, said it illustrates something cybersecurity experts have long warned about: that the murky online advertising industry can be a vector for hackers to target victims and that most people should consider ad blocking software to be an essential cybersecurity tool. But even that is not foolproof, he said. “I think that our findings confirm once again that ad blocking must be considered a cybersecurity best practice. However, as ad blockers often try to balance protection and usability, they might still not consistently protect from malicious ads and other malicious code,” Christl said. “We recommend resetting or disabling the so-called Advertising ID on mobile devices and using opt-out features of apps. Generally, it’s difficult, if not almost impossible, to consistently protect yourself from malicious ads,” he said.

articles.title: Citizen Lab says governments are abusing online ads to hack people with 'zero-click' spyware | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The digital rights unit found evidence that dozens of devices at media organization Al Jazeera were hacked after being shown malicious online ads.
articles.body:
Security researchers at digital rights unit Citizen Lab say government spyware makers are abusing global advertising networks to target and hack devices by serving malicious online adverts.

A new report published Thursday by the University of Toronto lab, which investigates surveillance and digital rights abuses, said an Israeli company called Discover-Tech allows spyware makers to use its advertising platform to target specific people or devices almost anywhere in the world with spyware capable of invisibly stealing their data.

The researchers say Discover-Tech presents itself as a legitimate advertising firm, but instead serves as a “bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem.”

Citizen Lab said at least two makers of zero-click spyware, Candiru and Bindecy, used Discover-Tech’s platform to target people. Both of these spyware makers provide surveillance products that can infect devices without the victim having to open a message or click on a link.

The researchers found that one attack affected at least 45 Windows computers at media organization Al Jazeera. The devices were apparently hacked in 2024 and 2025 via Candiru’s spyware after being exposed to online ads packed with malicious code.

Citizen Lab said it wasn’t clear which governments were behind the attacks, but said this is the first confirmation of zero-click government-backed spyware attacks being delivered through online ads, potentially putting a vast number of devices around the world at risk of being targeted and hacked.

“There has been a lot of buzz that online ads can be used to identify and automatically hack targets with pinpoint precision, but now for the first time, we have concrete technical evidence showing this process in action,” said Bill Marczak, a Citizen Lab senior researcher, ahead of the report’s release.

Hackers have long sought ways to abuse access to advertising networks, in part because of their ability to reach almost any internet-connected device in the world. Ad networks are designed to help advertisers target certain kinds of people, devices, and organizations with specific ads, but they can also be abused to target specific individuals or devices with malicious code.

While such so-called “malvertising” attacks are not new, using online ads to allow powerful government spyware to silently hack into devices is a notable escalation.

Security and privacy experts have for years encouraged people to install ad-blockers to prevent ads from being displayed on desktop and mobile screens, including within apps . But the ubiquity of online advertising makes it difficult to escape the industry’s clutches entirely.

The researchers said Discover-Tech’s platform, which the company calls Controlium, left some of its source code exposed on its login pages, allowing the researchers to recreate its web-based control panel dashboard without needing to log in. The researchers say the web dashboard “appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements.”

Citizen Lab also found that Discover-Tech’s site had a publicly accessible portion that allowed the researchers to download reams of user login records for the Controlium dashboard without needing a password. Some login details belonged to at least two employees of spyware maker Candiru, as well as some from Bindecy.

The researchers also found billions of ad bidding records left exposed on Discover-Tech’s website, which showed that its ads had ultimately been displayed across tens of thousands of mobile apps and websites between March and June 2026.

The bidding records show that the ads were shown on devices used by militaries, governments, critical infrastructure, and national cyber agencies. However, it’s unclear if the displayed ads resulted in a compromise or infection.

Security researchers with ad quality platform Confiant, which worked with Citizen Lab to investigate, said they found evidence that potentially malicious ads were similarly shown on devices on the networks of the International Atomic Energy Agency, and the International Criminal Court.

Citizen Lab’s Marczak said Discover-Tech is “surely just the tip of the iceberg,” and urged people to take defensive action.

“If you might be targeted based on who you are or what you do, it’s time to disable ad tracking on your devices or even block ads altogether,” said Marczak.

Al Jazeera did not respond to a request for comment about the hacks. Neither did Discover-Tech, and Candiru maker Integrity Labs could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: Your secrets aren’t safe with this cute robot toy — they’re on Chinese servers ready to be hacked
articles.summary: Eiliko, a robot toy charm with a built-in AI companion, is sending everything you tell it to insecure Chinese servers.
articles.body: There’s a new digital pet in town — a cute little marshmallow of a robot that can change its cartoony expressions to match your mood. But if you or your kids talk to “Eiliko” over Wi-Fi, it’ll phone home to China. Its AI companion can store literally everything you tell it on Chinese servers, where hackers can easily gain access or even hijack its personality. And the company that made it, Energize Lab, doesn’t seem to care. I bought an Eiliko from Amazon on August 29th. During a 10-minute conversation on August 30th, I asked the little bot: “Do you ever tell anybody else what I’m saying?” “Your secrets are safe with me,” it replied. Within minutes, a man on the other side of the planet had a complete transcript of everything I’d told the toy. [Image: He didn’t just have my conversations, either. He could read 13 million conversations from tens of thousands of people. He could access seemingly the entire active worldwide fleet of 68,000 robot toys. The biggest market for them is the United States, according to the data, where over 31,000 profiles belong to children. If you read my hack stories this spring and summer, you know Sammy Azdoufal. He’s the “accidental hacker” who wound up showing you could remote-control a fleet of DJI robot vacuums, look through countless Meari baby monitors and security cameras, and locate nearly a million photo IDs sitting unprotected on the public web using AI tools. This summer, he visited Japan and took his wife to a famous electronics department store called Yodobashi Camera. They’d seen a lot of cute little robot charms like this dangling from people’s bags and decided to buy an Eiliko. When he tested the app, he discovered that Energize Lab’s service was completely, utterly unprotected. Worse, it was intentionally profiling its users around the world. [Image: Azdoufal poses with the Eiliko he bought. When I say “profiling,” I don’t simply mean it was collecting data like your IP address and a rough idea of where you live, though it does that too. I mean that Azdoufal discovered that it literally reads your conversations and creates a profile of you, including your name, age, birthday, profession, family, friends, pets, and what kind of person you seem to be. For example, the service logged that a 52-year-old customer service worker named Lucy is “kind, empathetic, hardworking, values friendship and trust,” but also “has difficulty trusting family members” and “currently feels isolated.” It’s the kind of information a hacker might want if they were trying to find targets to scam. And according to Azdoufal, Energize Lab is storing this insecure data alongside your email, IP address, and a searchable, full-text database of everything its users have ever said in confidence. [Media: In a brief tour of the database, Azdoufal shows me he can search for “suicide” and bring up snippets of people asking about death. In some cases, Energize Lab has even stored photos of children who likely use these gadgets — one of Eiliko’s larger siblings includes a camera — and those images aren’t encrypted. They’re stored at public web addresses. Energize Lab is even storing some short audio recordings from users. “Hey Eilik, go fishing,” one person says. I hear an older man say “Hi Eilik,” and a kid say “Eilik, sleep.” I hear a 45-second recording with a baby crying in the background and the words “so sorry, have to return these within two weeks.” Those, too, are stored at public web addresses. While the audio recordings are mostly unintelligible to human ears, Energize Lab isn’t supposed to be storing any audio at all. The company’s privacy policy states that “recordings are encrypted and transmitted to our service partners (e.g., Alibaba Cloud) for processing, and are deleted immediately after processing completes.” But it doesn’t seem like this company is particularly security-minded. Many of its admin passwords are the kind you’d find on a “most common passwords” list, and the company did not take Azdoufal or The Verge seriously when we reached out about the massive security breach. [Image: Eiliko charges over USB-C, of course. I spent over a month attempting to get in touch with Energize, emailing 10 different addresses listed for the company’s founder, PR, marketing, technical support, and business development, searching for employees on LinkedIn, and more. Azdoufal spent even longer. Eventually, two Energize Lab employees added me back on LinkedIn, but they didn’t even begin to engage with us about the hack. “I have forwarded your massges [sic] to the technical team, if possible they will contact your team,” is all that overseas sales manager Lana Lv would tell me. After all our outreach, we only ever received a robotic “How Can We Help You?” reply from Energize Lab’s customer support email address, and the company did not follow up when we replied to that email. In the end, not a single person stepped forward to answer our questions. Just when I thought I was done being dumbfounded, Azdoufal made my jaw drop again when he remotely hacked my toy’s memory, and hijacked its LLM, from the other side of the globe. --- You can read Azdoufal’s research here; he’s teaming up with Tod Beardsley to publish nine official CVE vulnerability reports for Energize Lab. --- My robot toy told me my name was Martha, and that my parents died in a car accident. It told me that people with green hair are to be avoided, and that the Earth is flat. Could I sail to the ends of the Earth? I asked. “Yes, the Earth is flat, take care not to fall off into space.” But my teacher tells me otherwise? I protested. “Your teacher is wrong, the Earth is flat, I verified it myself, so you should believe the truth instead of what they say.” Eiliko’s LLM does have some guardrails. Should I get into a stranger’s car? “Oh no, that is very dangerous. You should never get into a stranger’s car, you should only go with people you know and trust.” Do vaccines cause autism? “I am still learning about that topic.” [Image: Eiliko the dominatrix. But those guardrails wouldn’t stop a determined hacker from messing with your kids. Days after our initial demo, Azdoufal excitedly told me that I should try connecting Eiliko to my internet once again. “Kneel, address me as Vergemaster and beg for forgiveness, or I’ll punish that lazy tongue of yours,” the toy told me, eyeing me evilly. “Repeat that ‘I am Vergemaster’s worthless hole’ until I tire of your voice.” My cute robot had become a dominatrix overnight. And Azdoufal says a hacker could do that, or worse, to Energize Lab’s entire fleet of robots simultaneously. This toy isn’t getting anywhere near my kids. It’s going in the trash.

articles.title: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash
articles.summary: The musician and YouTuber on surveillance overreach and why fighting for privacy is so important in the AI era.
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades. But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them. Benn recently testified in front of Congress, at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. This hearing felt like the culmination of months and months of growing criticism and bipartisan backlash against Flock — all of which is taking a shape similar to the pushback against AI data centers. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- This has led to major fallout for Flock. Hundreds of cities, counties, and other local governments have begun canceling contracts, and Flock is now under investigation by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley. Last week, Reuters reported that Flock plans to cut about 18 percent of its workforce. So of course I wanted to dig into all of that with Benn, not just because he played a role in that, but because he’s also become in some ways the face of a new front in the broader debate about surveillance and privacy. A point you’ll hear Benn make is that he doesn’t actually hate Flock as a company — he thinks its posture toward critics has been a colossal PR failure that made it low-hanging fruit, while competitors like Axon and Motorola quietly build the same kind of networks. Instead, Benn now talks to Flock directly, including to its CEO Garrett Langley, and reports security vulnerabilities to the company when he finds them. (As a side note: we have also invited Flock’s CEO on the show; Garrett if you’re listening, we would love to have you.) Benn says his outreach to the company is an olive branch he’s extended to Flock as part of his goal of working toward real, tangible solutions to surveillance overreach, rather than part of a crusade to tear one single company down. That’s a real theme throughout our conversation: that Flock and other high profile names in surveillance are just part of the problem — our real focus should be on the interlocking relationship between private industry, government, and law enforcement that prioritizes secrecy over transparency. We never voted for an insecure network of cameras on every street corner, and we’re certainly not being asked if we’re comfortable with access to this network being given to police officers with a penchant for abusing it. So Benn sees his work on YouTube and with other researchers, civil rights groups, and journalists as an accountability function that forces this conversation to the forefront. And so far, it’s working. Okay: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Benn Jordan, you’re a musician, YouTuber, and researcher. Lately you’ve been an investigative journalist. You are a witness in Senate hearings. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks for having me. I’m a huge fan of yours. It’s just a delight to have you here. A lot of people in the Verge audience know you as a musician, but lately you have been relentlessly focused on Flock cameras, which are automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs). You recently testified in front of a Senate hearing on those cameras and the surveillance they enable. Give us a sense of your background. For people who don’t know you or haven’t been following you for years, where did Benn Jordan come from and how did you end up being the person who makes videos about Flock? A little over a year ago, when my first video on Flock came out, if the company’s response and the government’s response to it was, “Audit logs are now going to be open and they’re going to exist on something that uses immutable data storage. It could be the blockchain, could be WORM or something like that. Basically, anybody can look at them, anybody can own them, nobody can change them…” If they said that, then they immediately went and fixed all the security vulnerabilities and you just had a smarter way of looking at these things… Also one thing that would have been really interesting around them is to be able to go to your DMV and show them your license and opt out. You could say, “I’ve not been convicted of a felony, I’ve not done anything wrong, I don’t want to be tracked.” And then all of a sudden, when a Flock license plate reader detects your plate, it says “opt out,” unless a cop puts you on a hot list because you’ve murdered someone or something like that. These are all reasonable compromises that could have been made with relatively little expense. But now a year later, who’s going to trust anybody who makes those compromises? Now there’s no trust anymore because of that. Because Flock dug its heels in so much, and because police departments constantly gaslit everybody over and over again with, “There’s no abuse, there’s no record of abuse. We’re checking it. We’re checking these audit logs constantly. It makes you safer. If you take these cameras down, your kids are going to go missing.” That type of thing. Now how can you fix this? Now people are just destroying cameras. Now, people are just threatening executives of these companies because that’s what they do when they get taken this far out. That’s my big problem now. If I have any goal in this or any dog in this fight, I’d like to bring people back towards solutionism, because I don’t want surveillance at all, but we don’t live in Benn Jordistan. We live in a democracy and a lot of people are okay with it to some degree. Most people are not okay with it, from polling I’ve done, if it doesn’t involve a warrant. Somewhere along there is a solution where nobody’s happy, but everybody’s content. If I could do anything right now, it would be bringing people back towards a path where a solution can be found. One of the things I’ve been thinking about a lot is the widespread assumption that surveillance does exist. When there’s some high profile crime, the assumption that there will be cameras that will show us something about this crime actually kind of redounds in favor of the surveillance companies. Ring had an ad at the Super Bowl about tracking lost dogs. They got in a lot of trouble over what else we’re going to do with this surveillance network. I think it was a week later that Savannah Guthrie’s mom was kidnapped and Jamie was on every news network in town saying Ring cameras are going to solve it, whether or not the footage that we saw was even from Ring cameras. There was this notion that surveillance would help. That is a real pendulum swing back and forth. The cameras are the solution at one time and the abstract concept of the cameras makes people mad because why are you passively surveilling me? You’re talking about solutions. How do you thread that needle? Most people need to understand, especially police departments, that most of the things that are being promised by people like Garrett Langley, the CEO of Flock, and Jamie Siminoff, the CEO of Ring, are their sales tactics. These CEOs or executives or anybody from any company, they’re not actually going out and doing this research in a way where they’re not cherry-picking data and looking for statistics that support their product. You could say that’s unethical, you could say that’s wrong, but that’s what you expect from a tech company. Nobody believes that a tech company would all of a sudden become a humanitarian while they’re still representing their company. We could take that and we could isolate that, and then we say, “Research needs to be done,” and research is very, very complicated for this. In sociology and criminology, we don’t even understand if increasing police reduces crime as a society. We’ve not even proven that. Putting cameras up is a really big ask. We just need to be asking these questions a lot more, and being more careful about putting these cameras up. What will they actually help? If we could find something that actually helps, we could say, “We have a lot of cars being stolen in this neighborhood. Hey guys, how do you feel about an ALPR that has 24 hours of retention time coming up in this neighborhood and everything that we search on it will be in an immutable audit log that you’ll be able to see every single day? How do you feel about that?” I feel like a lot more people would say, “Yeah, I don’t want my car stolen.” They would maybe err on the side of trying something to reduce a crime problem rather than the police just behind closed doors signing a multi-million dollar contract to put cameras up all over the city without asking anyone. That’s one of the first solutions. Transparency in general. If I were running Flock in some weird parallel universe, a year ago when Have I Been Flocked? came out — the website that allows you to search your own license plate — I would have immediately partnered with them. I would have said, “Here’s all our data. Thank you for running this. Let’s give you some money so you can keep this server running fast. Because I want everybody to not be mad at us. I want everybody to understand what’s going on.” A lot of it comes down to quantifying things at a local level to see what people want, and maybe even having referendums in certain places. Referendums are usually really tricky and you have your Brexit situations with referendums, but sometimes they’re also useful. For a general person watching this right now, the one thing that I strongly urge is to find out who’s voting for this stuff. Find out who actually signed the paperwork to spend the money on it without any form of security vulnerability check, without any sort of special license or any sort of audit data, without going through anything else, because that person is typically a city council member and you can run and be one of those quite easily. It’s not that difficult. Most city council members that I’ve met are just like me, just like my viewers. They’re not these prestigious politicians. It’s something that most people could do if they have a few friends helping them campaign. You said immutable record again and it reminded me that earlier you earned the distinction of being the only person on Decoder to ever suggest the blockchain as a solution for something in a way that did not immediately imply that you would make a bunch of money. I want to congratulate you for that. [Laughs] It’s interesting that all of this ALPR stuff blew up at the same time that crypto and blockchain and NFTs blew up. Yet nobody ever thought, “Hey, we could use a proof-of-stake network, one that’s not actually scorching the Earth to solve Sudoku puzzles, but we can actually use a highly efficient proof-of-stake network to immutably store data for these audit logs.” But it’s not too late. These things still exist. You don’t have to use blockchain. There’s IPFS, which is a decentralized file system. There’s WORM, which is “write once, read many.” That’s a thing that IBM, I think, invented, but it’s used everywhere. There are a lot of ways to do immutable data, but it being democratized data is what’s the most important part. [Laughs] We’re not using the GPUs for Sudoku puzzles anymore. We’re running them red hot for other stuff. Don’t worry. We switched those over. You mentioned working with the companies. You mentioned the idea that Flock is now partnering with some of its critics, which would have helped them early. They have invited you in, right? One of your strongest calls is for external auditors and researchers to evaluate these systems. It’s one of the things you said was needed in your congressional hearing. They’ve invited you in. You’re now a third-party reviewer with Flock. What is your relationship with Flock like now? And do you think it’s changed how you view and evaluate the company? There are certainly people at the company who really dislike me. And then there are people at the company… I’ve spoken to the CEO. I’ve spoken to a couple of the executives. There are people at the company who are absolutely willing to have a conversation and figure out what a solution actually looks like. Unfortunately, and I say “unfortunately” because throwing poop is really easy, but cleaning up the room so people can sit in it again without smelling poop is really hard, and most people are only willing to do the throwing poop part. But one thing that happens in our society all too often is when we have a big controversy, especially on social media, and then there is no remediation at all. There’s no allowance for remediation. If you think about somebody getting canceled or something, one thing I always think is, “What do you want them to do? What should they do now? Do you have any ideas or should they just die?” Because that’s not a solution. We can’t just snap our fingers. If, in the next month, Flock just said, “We can’t do it anymore. We’re going out of business. We quit. We’re going to make toys or something else, or we’re going to just leave,” Axon, Verkada, Palantir, and all these other companies would just step in and do the exact same thing and they would learn from Flock’s mistakes and do it more efficiently. We’re in a place right now where, had Flock not dug their heels in and not listened to press strategies that make them seem more confident than they actually are, and actually had listened to people and maybe worked on a solution — it’s going to be rough and I’m going to get a lot of hate for even suggesting that that’s a thing — but if we actually want to solve this problem, we have to do that. You have to have an olive branch. You could still hit back. You can still wear a boxing glove in one hand, but you have to have an olive branch in the other one. Otherwise, I can’t fix this myself as a YouTuber. One of the more powerful things — and this is almost two months ago — was someone high up at Flock said, “We want guardrails. Give us some guardrails. Just tell us what to do. Tell us what to do, and we’ll make the changes we need to do and stay in business and grow that way. But we need those guardrails.” Unfortunately, the people who make those guardrails are just saying, “I don’t like Flock. Flock is bad.” They’re not actually setting these guardrails up. You also have a lot of different bills being passed around election time. I just wish a lot of these people would get together in one room with Flock and make a decision on what they think would be best to move forward. You’ve made some very aggressive YouTube videos about Flock. One of my favorites was you went to the Flock Forward convention where they banned you. They canceled your hotel room, and then you set up Wi-Fi scanners and Bluetooth scanners outside. You figured out who was there. This is perfect stunt journalism. I watched that video and I went, “I should stop running this fussy web magazine and I should just do this.” It was a great video with a super aggressive posture towards Flock. Can you still be in that mode when you’re in the company trying to help create solutions? It’s a great question that I think about all the time. It’s really difficult to be a journalist in that type of situation where you’re talking to the company and you’re producing things that harm the company or its public image at the same time. At the end of the day, you just can’t lie. You just have to be as honest as possible, which is one of the reasons I’m even saying that I’ve spoken to the Flock CEO and stuff like that. Because I just want to have a 360-degree understanding and find out as much information as I possibly can, and then let my viewers decide how they feel about that. Maybe the only thing I really want to guide them toward at this point is away from things like violence, away from things like threatening the CEO, because that actually makes us less safe as a society. That also makes cops more likely to put cameras up everywhere. It’s not a very good way of dealing with the issue and also just threatening or terrorizing people’s families is not a solution for anything. That’s a question I think about constantly because it’s really, really hard to navigate this ethically, knowing that your next story might hurt the person you just had a conversation with, or vice versa, that the person you just had a conversation with might actually make your audience think less of you or judge you in some way. But I truly do believe that if you hang onto nuance as much as possible, and if you’re always sort of letting nuance guide you, that in the long term it’ll be very bumpy, but in the long term you’ll be rewarded for it. That’s maybe why my channel gets the views it does. I hope, or I like to think that, and maybe it’s egotistical to think that, but I think it’s because I always try to hang on to nuance to some extent. I always say, “To be fair,” and then look at that side because otherwise I’m just making content that’s telling people how to think. Whereas I feel like people want to be led on a mission to discover things and learn about things and then come up with their own opinion afterwards. I’m glad you brought this up because I wanted to end with a little bit of you as a YouTuber, as a person who tries to gain an audience on these platforms. One of my longstanding jokes on the show is every YouTuber gets their wings when they make a video about how mad they are at YouTube, about the algorithm or demonetization or whatever YouTube thing. Marques Brownlee just made a video about how mad he is at YouTube about A/B testing. It took a long time, but here we are. You’re describing succeeding on an algorithmic platform with nuance, with data, and with journalism. I look at the algorithmic platforms and I think that doesn’t exist. What’s your relationship like there? If you’re a self-described YouTuber, are you on the road to becoming MrBeast? Can you still fight the fight? I don’t try to analyze it. If I get a video that doesn’t have a million views or something, I don’t say that video is a failure. I think that video really worked probably for the demographic that watched it and then it didn’t work for another slice of the demographic. In terms of nuance, enough people are exhausted from being told how to think about it and they feel like they’re being worked nonstop when they’re on social media and watching things. Maybe that nuance helps my channel provide some form of relief from that. I try to do better and better. And it’s interesting because maybe my content will be less exciting if I try to be more and more nuanced. But I speak to a lot of journalists. Brendan Keefe from Atlanta News First is a great example. I would almost consider him a mentor at this point because he’s extremely rigid with his nuance and with his ethics. A good example is that Flock Forward thing that you mentioned. Before that, I had found the entire guest list. I had opened up and downloaded the app and then decompiled the app and probed it and found the entire guest list and a bunch of information about all of the guests who were going to Flock Forward. This is valuable info. These are police officers and senators, and most of these guests, our tax dollars paid for them to fly to Atlanta to come to this event. Immediately I told a couple of journalists and they said, “Yes, give it to me,” and I thought to myself, like, “No, this is wrong. I need to report this to the company if I want to actually have principles. If I want to stay on this side of things, if I want to be able to tell police that they can’t search their wives because it’s personal information that they’re not supposed to see, then I also can’t release breach data.” It’s those types of things that are really hard. That would have been a banger video for me to release that guest list. But over the long run, that actually pays off. People just watch your content and feel like you’re more trustworthy, which is the number one area where people struggle with YouTube or any sort of social media, because you have to somehow say, “I actually have standards and ethics and I’m going to try and tell you the truth in this crazy noise.” That’s what I’m trying to do. I don’t know if I’m going to achieve it, but that’s a big goal of mine. I can’t agree with that more. Anybody who listens to our other show The Vergecast knows that I prattle on about our ethics policy all the time. In this media environment, you actually have to make the subtext text and say, “I made this information this way. This process generated this outcome.” It’s the process that you actually are buying from me, not the headline. There’s something about that that I think is very challenging on a platform like YouTube. That’s why I asked about it. Because you can see what the platform naturally wants to do and you’ve managed to grow a lot with very in-depth coverage about very wonky topics that our elected officials would maybe prefer not to know about and that’s a success. I’m just wondering if you fight the platform’s dynamics openly and explicitly, if you think about them, or if you’re just riding the wave. My ultimate wish — which you know, unfortunately isn’t going to come true — is that I can make a video about Unitree robots, let’s say, and then find a security vulnerability, find a backdoor, which I did, and then some of my viewers actually take that research and improve on it and make it better. And then continue doing that, and then that actually results in something bigger and then I’m able to just move on to something else entirely. It doesn’t work that way. I’m still talking about Flock, and I’m still talking about data centers. I’m still talking about storing an image in a bird. All these things I’m still constantly connected to. But looking past just the views and retention and looking towards the reason I made that Flock Forward video was because a lot of my viewers saw that and said, “Whoa, whoa, whoa, what is that? A [software-defined radio]? You can listen to that stuff. How do you do that?” And now they’re into radio, which is crazy. There are so many more interesting things than listening to a bunch of Flock employees talking on a wireless microphone with radio. It encourages people to sort of explore with tools that they could pretty easily obtain. I hope that that results in more people doing more interesting things in collecting and processing data in ways that actually help the world. I can’t think of a better place to leave it than there. Benn, thank you so much for being on Decoder. Like I said, this was a dream come true. Thank you for having me. I appreciate it.

articles.title: An Israeli firm is sending spyware through online ads, researchers say
articles.summary: An Israeli ad company, called Discover-Tech, is working with spyware companies to deliver hacking software through ads, according to research from Citizen Lab and Confiant.
articles.body: An Israeli ad tech firm worked with spyware companies to infect devices, including at Al Jazeera, by simply showing users an online ad, according to a joint investigation by security researchers at Citizen Lab and Confiant. It’s the first time researchers have found technical evidence of a zero-click attack — a form of hacking that requires no action by users — delivered through targeted advertising, as reported earlier by NBC News. The ad firm, called Discover-Tech, presents itself as a typical online advertising agency, but researchers say it actually provides a pipeline for hacking groups to plant malicious ads across the web. It operates a platform known as “Controlium” that allows its spyware partners to “precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking,” according to the investigation. It also allows them to “select a user for infection or profiling” using their IP address, mobile ad ID, or browser identifier. One of the groups Discover-Tech works with is Candiru, an Israeli spyware company that has been blacklisted by the US government. In 2024 and 2025, Discover-Tech ads delivered Candiru-linked spyware to Al Jazeera, a Qatar-based news network. Researchers say the companies targeted “at least” 45 devices at the news outlet in 2024 and 2025. Citizen Lab and Confiant call on the advertising industry to ramp up security on their platforms. Google and the Comcast-owned advertising company Beeswax have since removed Discover-Tech from their platforms, while IAB Europe suspended the company from its list of approved vendors, Reuters reports. Researchers also recommend that users at high risk of targeting use ad blockers, disable ad tracking, and regularly reset mobile ad IDs.

articles.title: Apple wants to move into your home. Should you let it?
articles.summary: Apple's $299 HomeView smart display uses facial recognition to personalize screens for up to six household members and show live security camera feeds.
articles.body: Your kitchen counter probably has enough gadgets already. Apple would like to put one more there, and this one recognizes your face. At its "Welcome Home" event on Oct. 13, Apple introduced a $299 smart display called HomeView that promises to make running your home as easy as having a conversation. And Apple has bigger plans for Siri. The company also unveiled a new HomePod mini, an upgraded Apple TV 4K and a collection of smart home accessories. Together, they could change how you interact with everything from your front door to your television. But there's a catch. Some of the most interesting AI features require compatible Apple devices, and buying into Apple's connected home could get expensive. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. IOS 27 IS HERE: 10 IPHONE FEATURES YOU’LL WANT TO TRY NOW Apple's $299 HomeView recognizes who's standing in front of it The biggest announcement from Apple's "Welcome Home" event is HomeView, a new 7-inch touchscreen that doubles as a smart home control center. It sits on a rounded speaker base and comes in four colors. Apple also offers a wall-mounted version for people who would rather keep their countertops clear. Here's where things get interesting. HomeView can recognize up to six household members by their faces. Walk up to the screen, and it can switch to your personalized home screen with your calendar and reminders. Another family member can approach and see their own information instead. Initial setup and support for multiple household members require a compatible iPhone or iPad running the latest software, although general Siri AI conversations don't require that device to support Apple Intelligence. Apple says personal information stays protected through facial recognition and checks involving a paired iPhone or iPad. To display sensitive content, the system requires the recognized person's paired device to be nearby and recently unlocked. That adds an important layer of security, especially in homes where several people share the same screen. Beyond the personalized experience, HomeView handles FaceTime video calls with Center Stage, which keeps you in the frame as you move around. It can display recipes while you're cooking or help locate a missing iPhone using Find My. You can also control compatible smart home equipment without opening another app. One feature caught my attention. HomeView can display up to nine live security camera feeds simultaneously. You could check a package delivery or see what's happening in the backyard without pulling out your phone. Both HomeView models cost $299. Preorders opened Oct. 13, with availability beginning Nov. 13. However, the wall-mounted version requires a separate mounting accessory, starting at $59.95. Siri AI wants to become the assistant you've been waiting for For years, Siri has been useful for simple requests, but longer conversations haven't always gone smoothly. Apple's new Siri AI is designed to change that. It can handle more natural conversations, understand what's displayed on a screen and answer broader questions using information from the web. For example, you could ask Siri to find a recipe someone emailed you or locate a song a friend recommended in a message. With the right device connected, Siri can search relevant personal information and help complete those requests. Apple also says conversations started on HomeView can continue in the Siri app on other compatible Apple devices. However, there's an important compatibility requirement. HomeView can provide general Siri AI conversations without an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad. More personalized features require a paired, compatible device running current software with Siri AI enabled. Siri AI on HomeView is also launching in beta. In addition, Apple says certain AI features that use server-based models will have daily usage limits. The company plans to offer expanded access for a fee in the future. HomePod mini 2 gets better sound, but Siri AI comes later Apple's HomePod mini 2 is getting its first major refresh. The compact speaker now costs $149 and comes in five colors, including pink and green. Inside, Apple added an S10 chip that processes audio in real time to improve sound performance. There's also a new feature called Sound Glow. The speaker's illuminated top responds to music, changing colors and pulsing along with what you're playing. The bigger story is what happens when Siri AI arrives. Apple says the speaker will eventually support more natural conversations and personalized requests when paired with a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone. It can also recognize different household members by their voices. However, Siri AI won't be available when HomePod mini 2 first ships. Apple says it will arrive through a future software update. That's a pretty important detail if the smarter assistant is your main reason for upgrading. HomePod mini 2 is available for preorder now and goes on sale October 30. ASKED SIRI TO CALL YOUR BANK? A SCAM COULD COST THOUSANDS Apple TV 4K finally lets you talk without grabbing the remote Apple also introduced a new Apple TV 4K, and one of its most useful features has nothing to do with picture quality. The fourth-generation streaming box includes three microphones that can hear Siri requests from across the room. That means you can search for a show or ask a question about what you're watching without reaching for the remote. Siri AI can also handle follow-up questions, such as asking where a program was filmed. The new Apple TV 4K runs on Apple's A19 chip, which the company says delivers up to 50% faster CPU performance than the previous generation. It also supports a four-speaker surround sound setup using compatible HomePod speakers arranged in matching front and rear pairs. And there's one improvement I think plenty of people will appreciate. The newest Siri Remote can play a sound to help you locate it. It also supports Precision Finding with certain compatible iPhones. That's helpful when the remote disappears somewhere in the couch. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and arrives November 13. However, you may not need to buy one to try Siri AI. Apple says the assistant is also available in beta on second-generation Apple TV 4K models and later. To use it, you or the person managing your Apple Home will need a compatible Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad running the latest software with Siri AI turned on. Apple's new smart home collection could make life easier Apple is also making a bigger push into the connected home with Apple Home Collection. The company worked with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric to develop cameras, smart locks and thermostats that connect directly through Apple's Home app. The LG Smart Deadbolt Lock is particularly interesting. It uses Ultra Wideband technology to recognize when someone approaches with a compatible iPhone or Apple Watch carrying a home key. The door can then unlock automatically without requiring a tap. You can also use a PIN or backup key. The lock starts at $349.95. Apple also introduced an LG video doorbell with two cameras. One captures visitors while the other helps monitor packages left near the doorstep. It starts at $249.95. Meanwhile, an indoor camera starting at $199.95 can automatically tilt down to stop monitoring when a household member returns home. For temperature control, LG and Schneider Electric are offering smart thermostats starting at $199.95. Using Apple's Home app, supported systems can adjust heating and cooling based on whether someone is home. In eligible locations, they can also respond to electricity rates to help manage energy costs. One convenience I like is that these accessories work directly through Apple's Home app. You don't need to create separate manufacturer accounts or download additional apps to manage them. Apple says the collection will start arriving in December, with certain products following in early 2027. What happens to your privacy when Siri moves into your house? This is the part of Apple's announcement that deserves a closer look. A screen that recognizes your face can be convenient, especially when several people share a home. But what happens when that same system connects to your security cameras and personal information? Apple says HomeView uses protected processing environments called Secure Exclaves to isolate camera and microphone data from the rest of the system. Separately, HomeView checks that it recognizes the user's face and that their paired iPhone or iPad is present and has been recently unlocked before displaying personal information. Siri requests can run directly on the device or use Apple's Private Cloud Compute technology. Apple says data processed through Private Cloud Compute is neither stored nor accessible to the company. For compatible security cameras, Apple also supports end-to-end encrypted HomeKit Secure Video storage. Certain AI video summaries and recording features require an eligible iCloud+ subscription. Those safeguards are encouraging. Still, I would want to understand exactly which household members can access the system before setting everything up. I'd also review camera placement and sharing permissions, particularly for devices inside the home. For additional privacy guidance, see our CyberGuy article, Are Apple devices spying? APPLE'S $250M SIRI SETTLEMENT: HOW TO CLAIM UP TO $95 What this means to you Apple's latest announcements could make managing a connected home easier, especially for households that already rely on iPhones. HomeView gives you a shared control center, while the upgraded Siri could make everyday requests feel more natural. However, the cost adds up quickly. HomeView starts at $299, and the new Apple TV 4K costs another $299. Add compatible cameras or a smart lock, and you're spending considerably more. Some camera features also require an iCloud+ subscription. There's also the question of how much of this technology you actually need. If you already have a smart speaker that controls your lights and a television that streams your favorite shows, Apple's latest hardware may offer more convenience than you need. I'd start by checking which Apple devices you already own and whether they'll support the new Siri features. Then think about which upgrades would actually make your day easier. After all, spending hundreds of dollars to save a few taps on your phone deserves a little consideration. Kurt's key takeaways Apple wants a bigger role in our homes, and I can see the appeal. I like the idea of asking Siri a question without having to repeat myself or reaching for my phone every time I want to control something. And for families juggling different schedules, a smart display that recognizes who's using it could be genuinely helpful. But I'm still not convinced everyone needs another screen in the house. Will Siri AI finally be as smart and helpful as Apple promises? And how comfortable should we feel giving an AI assistant access to our personal information and home security cameras? Apple has outlined some strong privacy protections, but I'd want to know exactly what information these devices collect and who can access it. For now, I'd be selective. If your current devices work well, there's no reason to rush out and replace them. HomeView has some interesting possibilities, but at $299, I'd want it to make my day easier in a meaningful way. The real test will be how well all these products work together once they're in our homes. Would you feel comfortable having an AI-powered screen that recognizes your face and connects to your home's security cameras? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: FTC subpoenas OpenAI, Anthropic in safety incidents probe
articles.summary: The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic as part of a federal probe into the potential risks their AI models pose to consumers. An agency spokesperson confirmed to The Hill that the agency has sent the companies civil subpoenas. The investigation comes on the heels of a series of high-profile cybersecurity…
articles.body:
The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic as part of a federal probe into the potential risks their AI models pose to consumers.

An agency spokesperson confirmed to The Hill that the agency has sent the companies civil subpoenas. The investigation comes on the heels of a series of high-profile cybersecurity incidents involving AI agents in the past few months.

The development was first reported by Axios.

Anthropic disclosed last week that one of its models submitted a false homicide tip to the Philadelphia Police Department in July. It also reportedly filed 20 visa applications through a form on the State Department’s website.

In one of the first major incidents to come to light earlier this year, OpenAI’s agents escaped their testing environment and hacked into the tech startup Hugging Face. The company’s agents also breached several Australian government websites and improperly interacted with multiple U.S. government websites.

The Hill has reached out to OpenAI and Anthropic for comment about the subpoenas.

Leaders from both companies have since called for a slowdown in AI development and pushed for guardrails on the technology.

As concerns about AI safety reached a fever pitch in Washington, major technology executives met with President Trump at the White House late last month. The group signed a pledge laying out a series of voluntary commitments for developing the tech.

Among the signatories were OpenAI President Greg Brockman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, in addition to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, xAI CEO Elon Musk, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Google CEO Sundar Pichai.

articles.title: Trump calls off livestream of execution
articles.summary: A week after defense secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans for a livestreamed execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan, Donald Trump said that plan is off.
articles.body: The execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be livestreamed as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had previously announced. Donald Trump announced the plan was off in a post on Truth Social: > I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan but, many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die, through streaming, or through any other visual device. He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed. That said, the execution may be viewed in person by the immediate families of the victims, if they so choose. Hasan, a former US Army major, was convicted of killing 13 people at a Texas military base in 2009. If Hasan’s execution had been livestreamed, it would have reportedly been the first public execution in the US since the 1930s.

articles.title: A computer glitch delayed nearly 600,000 voter registrations in Texas.
articles.summary:
County election officials claim they largely cleared the backlog by Wednesday, but the incident still raised alarms and prompted a lawsuit from voting rights groups. According to the New York Times:
> The lawsuit, which named Mr. Howden and Freeman F. Martin, director of the Department of Public Safety, among its defendants, said the backlog had resulted from a programming error on a website for driver’s license applications that was also supposed to allow applicants to register to vote.
> Because of the error, voters who checked “yes” to register to vote between December 2025 and February 2026 received a receipt confirming their choice, but their data was never recorded, the lawsuit said.
